title: Transformers and Attention
description: How self-attention works and why transformers power modern language models.

questions.prompt: In scaled dot-product attention $$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$ why are the scores divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$?
options: To keep the dot products from growing with $d_k$ and saturating the softmax
To make the output the same length as the input
To remove the need for the value matrix $V$
questions.explanation: If query and key entries have unit variance, their dot product has variance $d_k$. Without scaling, large scores push softmax into regions with tiny gradients.

questions.prompt: Self-attention on its own has no notion of token order, which is why transformers add positional information.
questions.explanation: Without positional information, permuting the input tokens just permutes the outputs. Positional encodings (sinusoidal, learned, rotary and others) inject order.

questions.prompt:
A decoder builds its attention mask like this:

```python
mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(n, n), diagonal=1).bool()
scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
```

Which positions can token $i$ attend to?
questions.explanation: `triu(..., diagonal=1)` marks everything strictly above the diagonal (future positions). Those get $-\infty$, so softmax gives them zero weight, leaving the current and earlier tokens.

questions.prompt: Which components appear in a standard transformer block?
options: Recurrent hidden state passed between tokens
questions.explanation: A block combines attention, a feed-forward network, and residual connections with normalization. Transformers process tokens in parallel and do not carry an RNN-style hidden state between positions.

questions.prompt: In self-attention, what role does a query vector play?
options: It selects which keys are relevant to the current position
It stores the final vocabulary logits
It encodes only the output token
questions.explanation: Queries are compared with keys to produce attention weights, which then mix the corresponding values.

questions.prompt: Why use multiple attention heads?
options: They can learn different representation subspaces or relationships
They eliminate the need for embeddings
They ensure every token has equal weight
questions.explanation: Separate heads apply distinct projections, allowing a layer to represent different interactions in parallel.

questions.prompt: A standard transformer encoder can use information from tokens on both sides of a position.
questions.explanation: Encoder self-attention is typically unmasked, so each token can attend across the full input sequence.

questions.prompt: In an encoder-decoder transformer, what does decoder cross-attention typically read?
options: The training labels at inference time
questions.explanation: Cross-attention uses decoder states as queries and encoder outputs as keys and values.

questions.prompt: For sequence length n, what is the usual time and memory scaling of dense self-attention scores?
questions.explanation: Dense attention forms interactions for pairs of positions, yielding O(n²) score and storage costs.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms can prevent a decoder-only language model from using future tokens during training?
questions.explanation: The causal mask blocks future context, and shifted targets train prediction of the next token. Position information is still useful.

questions.prompt: What is a key benefit of a residual connection in a deep transformer?
options: It provides a direct path for information and gradients
It forces attention weights to be uniform
It removes the need for nonlinear layers
questions.explanation: Adding a block input to its output supports signal and gradient flow through deep stacks.

questions.prompt: Layer normalization computes normalization statistics across the batch dimension by default.
questions.explanation: Layer normalization normally computes statistics over specified feature dimensions for each example, unlike batch normalization.

questions.prompt: What does a token embedding map represent?
options: A learned vector associated with a token ID
questions.explanation: The embedding table maps discrete vocabulary IDs to dense vectors learned during training.

questions.prompt: What is a common purpose of rotary positional embeddings?
options: Inject position-dependent rotations into query and key representations
questions.explanation: Rotary embeddings encode relative positional relationships through position-dependent rotations of attention vectors.

questions.prompt: During autoregressive inference, what is typically stored in a key-value cache?
questions.explanation: Caching prior keys and values avoids recomputing them at each generation step; gradients are not needed for inference.

questions.prompt: Which training objective is associated with a BERT-style masked language model?
options: Predict selected masked input tokens using surrounding context
Predict only the next token from left context
questions.explanation: Masked language modeling predicts hidden tokens using bidirectional context, unlike a strictly causal next-token objective.

questions.prompt: For finite attention scores, softmax attention weights are nonnegative and sum to one across the normalized axis.
questions.explanation: Softmax converts a score vector into a probability-like distribution over attended positions.

questions.prompt: What is the usual role of the position-wise feed-forward sublayer?
options: Apply nonlinear transformations independently at each token position
Mix information across positions using recurrence
Compress the vocabulary into one token
questions.explanation: The feed-forward network transforms each position separately; attention handles communication between positions.

questions.prompt: What is the typical purpose of fine-tuning a pretrained transformer?
options: Adapt its learned parameters to a target task or data distribution
Rebuild its tokenizer for every prediction
Guarantee correct outputs for unseen domains
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning continues training on task-relevant data, adapting a pretrained model but not guaranteeing generalization.

questions.prompt: What commonly happens to the outputs of multiple attention heads?
options: They are concatenated and linearly projected
They are averaged with the input token IDs
They are converted directly into labels
questions.explanation: A standard multi-head attention layer concatenates head outputs and applies an output projection to combine them.
